title: Coltrane, the acceptable face of the avant-garde
gist: On Coltrane's centenary, Max Mitchell traces how a once-derided avant-garde saxophonist (Larkin: jazz became 'ugly on purpose') became jazz's canonical, commercially durable figure, with A Love Supreme going platinum in 2021. He argues Coltrane uniquely brought meaning and ear-pleasing music into rule-free free jazz, aided by his identification with the Black political movements of the 1960s.

insights.claim: John Coltrane's 1965 album A Love Supreme was certified platinum for one million US sales in 2021, Blue Train went gold in 2001 and Giant Steps in 2018, decades after release.
insights.speaker: Max Mitchell
insights.so_what: Canonical jazz catalog keeps compounding sales for decades, supporting music-rights valuations.
insights.quote: In 2021, his 1965 magnum opus A Love Supreme was certified platinum for one million US sales

insights.claim: Coltrane's centenary, shared with Miles Davis, is being marked with concerts from the Barbican in London to the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles.
insights.speaker: Max Mitchell
insights.so_what: Anniversary events are recurring catalysts for catalog and live-event revenue.

insights.claim: A musician derided by critics like Philip Larkin and Clive James as ugly and absurd has become the 'acceptable face' of jazz, with a reputation now considered inarguable.
insights.speaker: Max Mitchell
insights.so_what: Contemporary critical consensus is a poor predictor of long-run cultural value.
insights.quote: ‘that jazz started to be ugly on purpose.’

themes.theme: Politics and meaning drive cultural adoption

insights.claim: Coltrane's refusal to bow to industry financial pressures endeared him to radical Black movements, and Miles Davis described him as their torchbearer in jazz.
insights.speaker: Max Mitchell
insights.so_what: Alignment with a political-identity movement can cement an artist's lasting cultural status.
insights.quote: He was their torchbearer in jazz
insights.locator: This determination to follow his calling

insights.claim: Clive James argued the political component of free jazz, Black dignity, made it impossible to argue against, but that the joy of the music was one of the sacrifices.
insights.speaker: Max Mitchell
insights.so_what: Political framing can insulate cultural products from aesthetic criticism.
insights.quote: the joy of the music was one of the sacrifices

insights.claim: Mitchell argues Coltrane's achievement was bringing real meaning, hope and ear-pleasing music into a postmodern rule-free artistic mode, a path few others have followed.
insights.speaker: Max Mitchell
insights.so_what: Durable avant-garde success requires accessibility alongside novelty.
insights.locator: But that was Coltrane’s great achievement

insights.claim: Greg Tate observed that by the early 1970s Coltrane's influence was felt everywhere in African American culture, from music and politics to religion, literature and food.
insights.speaker: Max Mitchell
insights.so_what: Shows the breadth of cultural spillover from a single artist.

insights.claim: Coltrane's breakthrough came via a 1955 call from Miles Davis for a Columbia session, and Giant Steps (1959) and My Favorite Things (1960) were the hinge albums before his turn to free jazz.
insights.speaker: Max Mitchell
insights.so_what: Mainstream hits gave him the platform to take avant-garde risks.

insights.claim: Coltrane's 1966 Japan tour, two decades after Pearl Harbor, was described by biographer Eric Nisenson as probably the greatest single triumph of his life.
insights.speaker: Max Mitchell
insights.so_what: Illustrates how fast former adversaries can become receptive cultural markets.
